# Motivation

## Motivation: Why simulate patients?

Robotic assistive devices could improve mobility after neurological injury,
but tuning their controllers takes long, costly human experiments.

::: {.fragment}
- The people who would benefit most are often least able to walk for hours
- Muscle-driven imitation learning (IL): train a policy to reproduce recorded
  walking on a musculoskeletal model, then use the simulation in place of the participant
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
The simulation is only as good as the muscle-level solution the policy finds.
:::

::: notes
**[~35 s]**

Robotic assistive devices could make a real difference in mobility after a
stroke or spinal cord injury. The bottleneck is tuning their controllers, which
takes long, expensive human experiments, and the people who would benefit most
are usually the least able to walk for hours.

*[click]* One alternative is muscle-driven imitation learning. We train a policy
to reproduce a person's recorded walking on a musculoskeletal model, and then
use that simulation in place of the participant.

*[click]* But the simulation is only useful if the muscle activity underneath
the motion is right, not just the motion itself.
:::

## Motivation: Kinematics can match while muscles don't

Healthy-gait benchmark: simulated muscle activation vs. measured EMG [@ahmad2026beyond]

```{=html}
<div class="bench">
  <div class="panel">
    <div class="ptitle">RMSE <span>(lower is better)</span></div>
    <div class="row"><div>HyFyDy</div><div class="track"><div class="bar hyfydy" style="width:41%"></div></div><div class="val">0.164</div></div>
    <div class="row"><div>MuJoCo</div><div class="track"><div class="bar mujoco" style="width:86%"></div></div><div class="val">0.344</div></div>
    <div class="axis"><span>0</span><span>0.2</span><span>0.4</span></div>
  </div>
  <div class="panel">
    <div class="ptitle">Correlation r <span>(higher is better)</span></div>
    <div class="row"><div>HyFyDy</div><div class="track"><div class="bar hyfydy" style="width:80%"></div></div><div class="val">0.40</div></div>
    <div class="row"><div>MuJoCo</div><div class="track"><div class="bar mujoco" style="width:22%"></div></div><div class="val">0.11</div></div>
    <div class="axis"><span>0</span><span>0.25</span><span>0.5</span></div>
  </div>
</div>
<div class="note">Pooled across muscles.</div>
```

::: {.fragment .takeaway}
Both frameworks tracked healthy kinematics, yet differed sharply in EMG fidelity.
Kinematic agreement is a weak indicator of correct muscle activity.
:::

::: notes
**[~40 s]**

We saw this directly in our healthy-gait benchmark. We trained two
state-of-the-art frameworks, HyFyDy and MuJoCo, to track the same healthy
walking, and compared their simulated muscle activations to measured EMG.

HyFyDy had a pooled RMSE of 0.164 and a correlation of 0.40. MuJoCo had roughly
double the error, 0.344, and almost no correlation, 0.11.

*[click]* Both tracked the joint angles, but they got there with very different
muscle activity. So kinematic agreement on its own tells us little about
whether the muscles are doing the right thing.
:::

## Motivation:The problem with pathological gait

::: {.two-col}
::: {.col}
[Healthy gait]{.label}

The imitation and effort objectives agree, since healthy walking is close to
metabolically optimal.
:::
::: {.col .fragment fragment-index=1}
[After stroke or incomplete SCI]{.label}

The kinematics come from inefficient neural drive, so the two objectives conflict.
:::
:::

::: {.fragment .takeaway fragment-index=2}
An effort-minimizing policy tracking patient kinematics may reproduce the joint
angles through a mechanism the patient does not use.
:::

::: notes
**[~35 s]**

In healthy walking that gap is manageable. The policy's reward combines an
imitation term and an effort penalty, and healthy gait is close to
metabolically optimal, so the two objectives point the same way.

*[click]* After a stroke or an incomplete spinal cord injury, they don't. The
patient's kinematics come from inefficient neural drive.

*[click]* So a policy that minimizes effort while tracking patient kinematics
may find an efficient way to reproduce the same joint angles, using a muscle
strategy the patient doesn't actually use. That's the core risk this project
tests.
:::

# Objectives

## Objectives and Hypotheses

Determine whether the wrong muscle solution occurs, how to detect it, and what
prevents it.

::: {.hyp-list}
::: {.hyp .fragment}
[H1]{.hyp-tag} Baseline policies track stroke kinematics but match EMG less closely
than matched able-bodied controls, especially on the paretic side.
:::

::: {.hyp .fragment}
[H2]{.hyp-tag} Synergy constraints improve EMG fidelity over the baseline without a
meaningful loss in kinematic tracking.
:::

::: {.hyp .fragment}
[H3]{.hyp-tag} Scaling the model to body dimensions improves tracking, with a smaller
effect on EMG fidelity than the controller change.
:::
:::

::: notes
**[~35 s]**

The goal is to find out whether that wrong muscle solution happens, how to
detect it, and what prevents it. We have three hypotheses.

*[click]* First, baseline policies will track stroke kinematics but match EMG
less closely than in matched able-bodied controls, and the gap will be largest
on the paretic side.

*[click]* Second, constraining the controller with muscle synergies will
improve EMG fidelity without meaningfully hurting kinematic tracking.

*[click]* Third, scaling the model to each person's body will improve tracking,
but will matter less for EMG fidelity than the controller change.
:::

# Methodology

## Methodology: 2 × 2 within-participant design

```{=html}
<table class="design">
  <colgroup><col style="width:22%"><col style="width:39%"><col style="width:39%"></colgroup>
  <thead>
    <tr>
      <th></th>
      <th>Generic model<span>default HyFyDy</span></th>
      <th>Scaled model<span>OpenSim scale factors → HyFyDy</span></th>
    </tr>
  </thead>
  <tbody>
    <tr>
      <th>Baseline controller<span>one command per muscle</span></th>
      <td>Existing pipeline, unchanged from the healthy benchmark
        <div class="h">H1: compared with matched controls</div></td>
      <td>Same controller on a body-scaled model
        <div class="h">H3: effect of scaling</div></td>
    </tr>
    <tr>
      <th>Synergy controller<span>a few synergy commands</span></th>
      <td>Muscle weights from the participant's own EMG; timing still learned
        <div class="h">H2: effect of the controller</div></td>
      <td>Both changes together
        <div class="h">Controller vs. model effect size</div></td>
    </tr>
  </tbody>
</table>
```

Every participant is run in all four conditions. Personalization is geometric only:
it does not model patient-specific weakness, spasticity, or muscle properties.

::: notes
**[~45 s]**

To test these, we use a two-by-two within-participant design. The rows are the
controller and the columns are the model.

The baseline controller outputs one command per muscle, which is our existing
pipeline unchanged from the healthy benchmark. Comparing it with matched
controls tests H1.

The synergy controller outputs only a few commands, mapped to muscles through
weights taken from the participant's own EMG. Going down a column is H2.

Going across a row, from the generic HyFyDy model to one scaled with OpenSim
scale factors, is H3. The bottom-right cell lets us compare the two effect sizes.

Every participant runs all four conditions. One caveat: personalization is
geometric only. We aren't modeling weakness, spasticity, or muscle properties.
:::

## Methodology: Data, controllers, and evaluation

```{=html}
<ol class="pipeline">
  <li><span>Data</span>Van Criekinge dataset; 5 stroke survivors, 5 matched controls</li>
  <li><span>Split</span>Training and held-out strides, before any synergy extraction</li>
  <li><span>Reference</span>Markers to reference motion; OpenSim scaling to HyFyDy</li>
  <li><span>Train</span>Imitation and effort reward, benchmark settings</li>
  <li><span>Evaluate</span>Simulated activation vs. EMG on held-out strides</li>
</ol>
```

::: {.two-col .small}
::: {.col}
[Synergy controller]{.label}

Non-negative matrix factorization per leg over six leg muscles, using the fewest
synergies that explain at least 90% of EMG variance. The policy still learns
when each group activates.
:::
::: {.col}
[Primary outcome]{.label}

EMG fidelity across the gait cycle, per muscle and per leg, with paretic and
non-paretic legs reported separately. Kinematic tracking is a necessary check,
not evidence of a correct muscle solution.
:::
:::

[Data: [@vancriekinge2023]. Synergy rationale: [@meyer2016synergies; @clark2010merging].]{.src}

::: notes
**[~45 s]**

We use the public Van Criekinge dataset: five stroke survivors, each paired
with a matched control. First, we split strides into training and held-out
sets, so the synergy weights never see the strides we evaluate on. Marker data
becomes the reference motion, and training uses the benchmark's reward.

For the synergy controller, we run non-negative matrix factorization per leg
over six leg muscles, keeping the fewest synergies that explain 90% of the EMG
variance. Timing is not prescribed; the policy still learns when each group
fires.

The primary outcome is EMG fidelity across the gait cycle, per muscle and per
leg, with paretic and non-paretic legs reported separately. Kinematic tracking
is a check we have to pass, not evidence of a correct muscle solution.
:::

```{=html}
<div class="timeline">
  <div class="step done"><i></i><div class="name">Dataset adopted</div><div class="desc">138 able-bodied adults and 50 stroke survivors; now the primary data source</div></div>
  <div class="step done"><i></i><div class="name">Feasibility run on stroke data</div><div class="desc">Model trained to walk on one stroke survivor's reference motion; not yet evaluated against their kinematics or EMG</div></div>
  <div class="step done"><i></i><div class="name">Synergies and scaling pipeline</div><div class="desc">Synergies computed for stroke participants; automated per-participant model scaling</div></div>
  <div class="step next"><i></i><div class="name">Evaluate first policy</div><div class="desc">Score it on the planned metrics and test the evaluation pipeline</div></div>
  <div class="step "><i></i><div class="name">Select and convert participants</div><div class="desc">Screen for EMG quality and usable strides on both legs</div></div>
  <div class="step "><i></i><div class="name">Train all four conditions</div><div class="desc">Baseline first, then synergy; all metrics on held-out strides</div></div>
  <div class="step "><i></i><div class="name">Validate on Shepherd Center data</div><div class="desc">Most informative conditions only</div></div>
</div>
<div class="tl-legend">Filled: done. Outlined: remaining.</div>
```

::: notes
**[~45 s]**

Here's where things stand. We adopted the Van Criekinge dataset, with 138
able-bodied adults and 50 stroke survivors, as our primary data source, and
trained the model to walk on one stroke survivor's reference motion. To be
clear, that shows feasibility only; we haven't yet evaluated it against their
kinematics or EMG. We've also computed synergies and automated model scaling.

Next, we score that first policy, which also tests the evaluation pipeline.
Then we select and convert participants, train all four conditions, and finally
validate the most informative ones on Shepherd Center data.

**[close, ~10 s]** In short, we're asking whether a simulated patient that
walks right is also using the right muscles, and what it takes to make it
so. Thank you, I'm happy to take questions.
:::
